key_points.point: The authors argue that the current focus on AGI as a 'North Star' is misguided and should be replaced by a focus on Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (SAI). They contend that humanity is not a paradigm of general intelligence but rather a collection of specialized adaptations, and AI should similarly embrace specialization. This perspective aligns with accelerationist goals by prioritizing the development of highly capable, specialized systems that can exceed human performance in important domains, rather than getting bogged down in the philosophical and technical quagmire of defining and achieving AGI. The authors emphasize that this shift will lead to clearer goals and more rapid progress in AI development.
key_points.verbatim: We argue that AI must embrace specialization, rather than strive for generality, and in its specialization strive for superhuman performance, and introduce Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (SAI).

key_points.point: The authors support the 'bitter lesson' that approaches scaling with computational power tend to outperform those based on domain knowledge. They argue that as scaling progresses, the need for domain-specific knowledge decreases, allowing for more powerful systems. This aligns with the accelerationist view that continued investment in compute and scaling is the primary path to achieving advanced AI capabilities. The authors qualify this by noting that while domain knowledge becomes less critical for the *construction* of the system, the system itself still benefits from specialization.
key_points.verbatim: We should also note that this claim does not dispute the bitter lesson (Sutton, 2019). The bitter lesson is the observation that approaches that scale with computational power tend to outperform ones based on domain knowledge, a claim that we agree with.

key_points.point: The authors argue that the current AGI discourse is fractured and polarized, largely due to imprecise terminology. They suggest that recentering the field around SAI will lead to better communication and faster progress. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of removing barriers to progress, in this case, conceptual ones. The authors acknowledge that the current confusion has led to extreme, polarized narratives that hinder productive research.
key_points.verbatim: We believe that recentering the discourse around SAI will lead towards better communication, clearer goals, and more rapid progress.

key_points.point: The authors argue that AI can be uniquely valuable by targeting domains where human cognition is systematically miscalibrated, such as high-dimensional statistical inference and complex mechanistic modeling. This supports the accelerationist view that AI is a tool for solving problems that are intractable for humans. The authors note that humans exhibit stable biases that are often error-prone in modern settings, which AI can overcome.
key_points.verbatim: Specialization also clarifies why AI can be uniquely valuable: it can target precisely the domains where human cognition is systematically miscalibrated.

key_points.point: The authors advocate for prioritizing operational definitions of intelligence that can be observed and measured, rather than getting stuck in philosophical debates about consciousness or subjective experience. This aligns with the accelerationist preference for pragmatic, engineering-focused approaches to AI development. They argue that internalist objections to AI intelligence reside in metaphysics and offer no falsifiable test for engineering progress.
key_points.verbatim: Our focus is on operational definitions—metrics that can be observed and measured—whereas the internalist objection currently resides in the realm of metaphysics and philosophy of mind, offering no falsifiable test for engineering progress.

key_points.point: The authors argue that the focus on human-level generality is an example of human-centric bias and hubris. They contend that AI should not be limited by human performance levels, but should instead strive for superhuman performance. This aligns with the accelerationist value of using AI to transcend human limitations. The authors acknowledge that human intelligence is a useful reference point during early development, but argue that anchoring benchmarks to human baselines is ultimately orthogonal to the route to superhuman capability.

The authors emphasize that competition acts as a selection mechanism that amplifies effective strategies and eliminates ineffective ones, similar to how entities in markets and organizations operate. This aligns with the accelerationist view that competitive dynamics are a powerful engine for progress. They argue that AI systems are not exempt from this pressure, and models that fail to meet performance thresholds will be neglected in favor of better-matched systems.

The authors propose that SAI can be realized through a hierarchy and diversity of models and modalities, rather than a single 'one paradigm to rule them all' approach. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of fostering diverse engineering approaches to accelerate progress. They note that the brain itself is a 'system of systems,' suggesting that AI architectures should follow a similar path to achieve fast adaptation.

The authors argue that world models are a useful mechanism for planning and zero-shot task transfer, which is a key component of SAI. This supports the accelerationist view that investing in specific architectural breakthroughs is the path to more powerful AI. They note that the physical world is too rich and stochastic for pixel-level prediction, and compact representations are necessary for effective dynamics forecasting.

The authors argue that the concentration of AI development in a few dominant architectures (like autoregressive LLMs) narrows the search space and slows progress. They advocate for a greater diversity of solutions to accelerate innovation. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of fostering a competitive and diverse AI ecosystem. They note that while shared tooling creates momentum, it also leads to local optima.

The authors argue that the goal of SAI is to adapt to tasks with human utility, which they define as a key metric for AI success. This aligns with the accelerationist view that AI should be focused on delivering practical, high-value outcomes. They note that the exact definition of utility is orthogonal to their arguments, but emphasize that focusing on utility is more practical than aiming for universal competence.

The authors argue that we should judge AI progress by its speed and efficiency in acquiring new skills, rather than by a checklist of fixed competencies. This aligns with the accelerationist focus on measurable progress and performance. They contend that individual skill testing is a 'Sisyphean endeavor' and that adaptation dynamics are a more robust measure of intelligence.

The authors argue that self-supervised learning (SSL) is a promising way to acquire generic knowledge, which is a foundational component of SAI. This supports the accelerationist view that investing in specific training paradigms is key to AI advancement. They note that SSL can be applied to any data with internal structure, making it highly scalable.

The authors argue that we should not be afraid of specialization, as it is a predictable consequence of limited resources and competing objectives. This aligns with the accelerationist view that we should focus on building the strongest available specialists. They note that the idea of a 'generalist mind' is a romantic notion that doesn't hold up to computational reality.

The authors argue that the current focus on AGI as the 'North Star' of the field should be replaced with an emphasis on adaptability. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of setting clear, achievable, and impactful goals for AI development. They contend that this shift will lead to better communication, clearer goals, and more rapid progress.

The authors acknowledge the existence of 'doomers' who fear a gruesome societal endgame, including mass unemployment and loss of human agency. While the authors themselves advocate for SAI, they recognize that the current discourse is polarized by these existential concerns. This matters from a safetyist perspective because it validates the seriousness of the risks being discussed, even if the authors propose a different path forward. The authors note that these extreme narratives are a significant part of the current AI debate.
key_points.verbatim: On one side are “doomers,” who argue we are headed towards a gruesome societal endgame— mass unemployment, loss of human agency, and a future in which humanity becomes subordinate to artificial overlords.

key_points.point: The authors acknowledge that current AI systems have limitations and can fail in novel environments, which is a key concern for safetyists. They note that humans are also specialized creatures with blind spots, and that AI can be uniquely valuable by targeting domains where human cognition is miscalibrated. This matters to safetyists because it highlights that AI is not inherently safe or perfect, and its failures can be significant. The authors qualify this by arguing that specialization is a predictable consequence of limited resources, not necessarily a sign of fundamental misalignment.

The authors argue that we should focus on building systems that can adapt to new tasks, which they define as SAI. This is a form of safety-by-design, as it emphasizes the importance of adaptability and learning efficiency. This matters to safetyists because it suggests that the focus should be on building systems that can handle novel situations safely, rather than just optimizing for performance. The authors note that this approach requires strong assumptions about the world, which is a key safety consideration.

The authors acknowledge that current AI systems, such as autoregressive LLMs, have flaws, including errors that diverge exponentially with prediction length. This matters to safetyists because it highlights the potential for cascading failures in AI systems. The authors note that these flaws are a reason to explore diverse architectures rather than relying on a single dominant paradigm.

The authors acknowledge that the AI community is fractured, with some framing AI as a 'normal technology' while others forecast extreme outcomes. This aligns with the skeptic's view that extreme narratives can be distracting. The authors themselves reject extreme narratives, framing AI as a tool that should be specialized and adaptable. This matters to skeptics because it grounds the discussion in practical engineering rather than speculative 'doomer' or 'utopian' scenarios.
key_points.verbatim: A third camp frames AI as a “normal technology,” forecasting major impacts but rejecting extreme narratives (Narayanan & Kapoor, 2025).

factual_claims.claim: The authors argue that human intelligence is not general, but rather a collection of specialized adaptations honed by evolution for survival.
The authors contend that there is no consensus on the definition of AGI in academia or industry.
The authors argue that the 'No Free Lunch' theorem implies that no single, general-purpose algorithm works best for every problem.
The authors state that recent self-supervised learning (SSL) models have reached state-of-the-art performance in most domains.
The authors argue that autoregressive language models exhibit errors that diverge exponentially with prediction length.
The authors claim that humans are incapable of performing tasks outside their evolutionary-honed range at a high level.
The authors argue that the current focus on generality as the 'North Star' of AI research is misguided.
The authors contend that AI systems that are 'too general' may suffer from negative transfer when tasks compete for representational capacity.
The authors argue that the brain is not a monolith but a system of systems, suggesting AI should follow a similar modular approach.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: The cognitive bias where humans perceive their own intelligence as general-purpose because they are unaware of their own evolutionary blind spots. It argues that humans are actually highly specialized for survival tasks and struggle with many others.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The authors argue that human intelligence is not a paradigm of generality but rather a collection of specialized adaptations. They contend that our perception of generality is an illusion caused by our inability to see our own limitations.
unmapped_concepts.reason: This concept challenges the foundational assumption of human-centric AI development across all camps.
